newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-IAAF VICE-PRESIDENT CRITICISES WILD CARD DECISION.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF VICE-PRESIDENT CRITICISES WILD CARD DECISION.

text.p: A top athletics official has slammed his own world body for allowing Michael Johnson to compete at the world championships despite not being selected by the U.S. team.
Arne Ljungqvist, International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) vice-president, said:"The decision-making process is completely mad.
"This is an important question on which a decision should be taken after full discussion and analysis, not through a flippant telephone vote with a few hours warning."
The IAAF announced earlier that it would be giving wild cards to defending champions for the first time at next month's championships in Athens.

Johnson, who completed historic 200 and 400 metres doubles at both the last world championships and at last year's Atlanta Olympics, was not selected for the U.S. team after he missed the national trials because of injury.
But like compatriots such as hurdler Gail Devers, sprinter Gwen Torrence and decathlete Dan O'Brien, who all missed or failed to finish the trials, he can now race.
Brad Hunt, the agent of Johnson, Torrence and O'Brien immediately confirmed that the trio would compete in Athens. "They will be there," he said.
Ljungqvist said the IAAF decision was "crazy" and he had abstained from the vote.
"I want no part of a voting procedure that looks like this and several others apart from me protested," he said.
It's a bit stupid when you adapt the IAAF rules to fit the Americans' rules. Its like putting the cart in front of the horse. The U.S. should fit its rules with those of the IAAF."
The wild cards, will also be given to champions at all world championships in the future and the idea is also set to be extended to indoor and cross-country championships.
If their national teams agree, defending champions will also be allowed to switch events. But, if that happens, each country will still only be allowed to field the maximum three athletes per event.

World 100 hurdles champions Devers, for example, could compete in the 100 metres in Athens if the United States agreed but the Americans would have to drop another sprinter from their women's 100 team.
Ljungqvist said he was surprised to hear that reigning champions could switch events.
"We were never asked that question so I do not understand how that conclusion can be drawn from the vote. The board cannot accept such a decision," he said.
The ruling largely affects the United States which has strict rules on qualification for major championships, allowing only the top three in the national trials to make the team.
The decision will certainly make their team much stronger and weaken the importance of the U.S. trials in the future.
It could also influence Kenyan and British athletes.

Britain's world triple jump champion Jonathan Edwards, who has been suffering with a heel injury, is now guaranteed his place at the event and does not need to prove his fitness to national selectors.
The IAAF also said that the host country of the championships would be allowed to enter one athlete in each event even if the athlete had not reached the qualifying standard for the discipline.
The changes were believed to have had the full backing of president Primo Nebiolo.
The body's ruling council was persuaded that it was a decision which would help the promotion of the championships which take place every two years.

Johnson, who is presently training in Texas after being injured in his 150-metre showdown with Canadian world 100 metres record holder Donovan Bailey earlier in the season, is planning to come to the world championships "to do something very special." Hunt said.
Hunt praised Nebiolo for pushing for the ruling.
"You have to give him a lot of credit," Hunt said. "He does understand how to present the sport so that it is seen and followed by as many people as possible.
